claim: Knockdown of SNAP in Drosophila Kc cells strongly reduces SOCE by day 3.
source: We found that knockdown of soluble NSF attachment protein (SNAP) strongly reduces SOCE by day 3 (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and referenced in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion in HEK-293 cells strongly inhibits SOCE by day three.
source: We depleted α-SNAP in HEK-293 (Figure 1B), Jurkat T cells (Figure 1C) and U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) using lentivirus-based RNAi constructs (Supplementary file 1) and found SOCE to be strongly inhibited by day three compared to cells treated with control RNAi.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion in Jurkat T cells strongly inhibits SOCE by day three.
source: We depleted α-SNAP in HEK-293 (Figure 1B), Jurkat T cells (Figure 1C) and U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) using lentivirus-based RNAi constructs (Supplementary file 1) and found SOCE to be strongly inhibited by day three compared to cells treated with control RNAi.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion in U2OS cells strongly inhibits SOCE by day three.
source: We depleted α-SNAP in HEK-293 (Figure 1B), Jurkat T cells (Figure 1C) and U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) using lentivirus-based RNAi constructs (Supplementary file 1) and found SOCE to be strongly inhibited by day three compared to cells treated with control RNAi.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and described in the text.

claim: By day five, depletion of α-SNAP causes cell rounding in adherent cell lines.
source: By day five, depletion of α-SNAP caused cell rounding in adherent cell lines; we therefore restricted our analysis to adherent cells at early time-points.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the text.

claim: Reconstitution of α-SNAP deficient HEK 293 cells with an RNAi resistant version of α-SNAP largely restores SOCE.
source: Importantly, when we reconstituted α-SNAP deficient HEK 293 cells with an RNAi resistant version of α-SNAP we found that SOCE was largely restored (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and described in the text.

claim: Defective SOCE in α-SNAP deficient HEK 293 cells can be restored by over-expressing β-SNAP.
source: Defective SOCE in α-SNAP deficient HEK 293 cells could also be restored by over-expressing β-SNAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and described in the text.

claim: γ-SNAP depletion does not inhibit SOCE in HEK 293 cells.
source: γ-SNAP depletion failed to inhibit SOCE in HEK 293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and described in the text.

claim: γ-SNAP over-expression does not compensate for α-SNAP depletion.
source: γ-SNAP over-expression did not compensate for α-SNAP depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion causes a strong reduction in nuclear translocation of endogenous NFATc1 in response to thapsigargin and PMA in Jurkat T cells.
source: Western blot of nuclear extracts of α-SNAP deficient Jurkat T cells showed a strong reduction in nuclear translocation of endogenous NFATc1 in response to the store-depleting agent thapsigargin (TG) in combination with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP is a novel regulator of SOCE and downstream signaling required for NFAT activation.
source: These data demonstrate that α-SNAP is a novel regulator of SOCE and downstream signaling required for NFAT activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: α-SNAP co-precipitates with Stim1 in store-depleted HEK 293 cells.
source: Co-immunoprecipitations (co-IPs) from lysates of store-depleted HEK 293 cells co-expressing either Stim1-Myc and YFP-α-SNAP (Figure 2A) or Flag-Orai1 and YFP-α-SNAP (Figure 2B) showed that α-SNAP co-precipitates with both Stim1 and Orai1 and vice versa.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP co-precipitates with Orai1 in store-depleted HEK 293 cells.
source: Co-immunoprecipitations (co-IPs) from lysates of store-depleted HEK 293 cells co-expressing either Stim1-Myc and YFP-α-SNAP (Figure 2A) or Flag-Orai1 and YFP-α-SNAP (Figure 2B) showed that α-SNAP co-precipitates with both Stim1 and Orai1 and vice versa.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B and described in the text.

claim: Purified α-SNAP directly binds to Stim1 in vitro.
source: To determine if the interaction is direct, we incubated 100 nM purified α-SNAP with Orai1 and Stim1 immunoprecipitates (IPs) in vitro. α-SNAP bound to both Stim1 and Orai1 but not to an unrelated calcium channel, TRPC6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: Purified α-SNAP directly binds to Orai1 in vitro.
source: To determine if the interaction is direct, we incubated 100 nM purified α-SNAP with Orai1 and Stim1 immunoprecipitates (IPs) in vitro. α-SNAP bound to both Stim1 and Orai1 but not to an unrelated calcium channel, TRPC6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: Purified α-SNAP does not bind to TRPC6 in vitro.
source: To determine if the interaction is direct, we incubated 100 nM purified α-SNAP with Orai1 and Stim1 immunoprecipitates (IPs) in vitro. α-SNAP bound to both Stim1 and Orai1 but not to an unrelated calcium channel, TRPC6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: Some α-SNAP co-localizes with Stim1 in almost all CFP-Stim1 expressing cells under resting conditions.
source: Some α-SNAP co-localized with Stim1 in almost all of the CFP-Stim1 expressing cells imaged even under resting conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D and described in the text.

claim: Upon store-depletion, distinct co-localization of α-SNAP with Stim1 clusters is observed in nearly 30–40% of cells.
source: Upon store-depletion, we observed distinct co-localization of α-SNAP with Stim1 clusters in nearly 30–40% of cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2E and described in the text.

claim: There is no obvious co-localization between α-SNAP and Orai1-CFP expressed alone under store-depleted conditions.
source: Although there was no obvious co-localization between α-SNAP and Orai1-CFP expressed alone under resting (not shown) or store-depleted conditions (Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2F and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP co-localizes at a higher frequency with clusters containing Stim1 as well as Orai1 in Stim1, Orai1 co-expressing stable cells, with nearly 75% cells showing distinct co-localization.
source: α-SNAP co-localized at a higher frequency with clusters containing Stim1 as well as Orai1 in Stim1, Orai1 co-expressing stable cells, with nearly 75% cells showing distinct co-localization (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 2G and described in the text.

claim: A part of the total cellular pool of α-SNAP constitutively binds Stim1.
source: Taken together, these data show that a part of the total cellular pool of α-SNAP constitutively binds Stim1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation data presented.

claim: Upon store-depletion, Stim1 likely brings α-SNAP to CRAC channel clusters where α-SNAP engages with Orai1.
source: Upon store-depletion, Stim1 likely brings α-SNAP to CRAC channel clusters where α-SNAP engages with Orai1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localization and binding data presented.

claim: Orai1-YFP localization is normal in α-SNAP depleted cells.
source: Epifluorescence imaging of Orai1-YFP and YFP-Stim1 expressing α-SNAP depleted cells showed normal localization of both Orai1 and Stim1 (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by epifluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A and described in the text.

claim: YFP-Stim1 localization is normal in α-SNAP depleted cells.
source: Epifluorescence imaging of Orai1-YFP and YFP-Stim1 expressing α-SNAP depleted cells showed normal localization of both Orai1 and Stim1 (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by epifluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3B and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depleted, resting, or store depleted cells do not show any significant difference in the levels of cell surface Orai1 when compared to controls.
source: α-SNAP depleted, resting, or store depleted cells did not show any significant difference in the levels of cell surface Orai1 when compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by BTX binding assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and described in the text.

claim: Immunostaining of α-SNAP depleted cells with an ER marker, calreticulin, shows no apparent changes in the ER morphology.
source: Consistently, immunostaining of α-SNAP depleted cells with an ER marker, calreticulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and a Golgi-marker, giantin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showed no apparent changes in the ER-Golgi morphology suggesting that at the time points used in our studies, α-SNAP depletion had not perturbed overall organelle structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and described in the text.

claim: Immunostaining of α-SNAP depleted cells with a Golgi-marker, giantin, shows no apparent changes in the Golgi morphology.
source: Consistently, immunostaining of α-SNAP depleted cells with an ER marker, calreticulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and a Golgi-marker, giantin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showed no apparent changes in the ER-Golgi morphology suggesting that at the time points used in our studies, α-SNAP depletion had not perturbed overall organelle structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and described in the text.

claim: At the time points used in the studies, α-SNAP depletion had not perturbed overall organelle structure.
source: Consistently, immunostaining of α-SNAP depleted cells with an ER marker, calreticulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and a Golgi-marker, giantin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showed no apparent changes in the ER-Golgi morphology suggesting that at the time points used in our studies, α-SNAP depletion had not perturbed overall organelle structure.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the immunostaining data presented.

claim: Expression of E329Q-NSF mutant blocks transferrin flux through the endocytic pathway by 8 hr.
source: We used inducible expression of a dominant negative NSF mutant, E329Q-NSF, which lacks the ATPase activity required for dissociating the SNARE complex (Dalal et al., 2004) and blocks transferrin flux through the endocytic pathway by 8 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 3C and described in the text, with citation to Dalal et al., 2004.

claim: SOCE is unaffected in E329Q-NSF expressing live and adherent cells even 20 hr after inducing the expression of the mutant.
source: Surprisingly, SOCE was unaffected in E329Q-NSF expressing live and adherent cells even 20 hr after inducing the expression of the mutant (Figure 3D and 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D and 3E and described in the text.

claim: WT-NSF fails to co-localize with Stim1 clusters in ER–PM junctions.
source: unlike α-SNAP, WT-NSF failed to co-localize with Stim1 clusters in ER–PM junctions (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 3F and described in the text.

claim: Reconstituting α-SNAP deficient cells with α-SNAP-L294A mutant fails to reconstitute transferrin flux through the endocytic pathway.
source: Most importantly, reconstituting α-SNAP deficient cells with a previously reported mutant of α-SNAP, L294A (Barnard et al., 1997) (Figure 4A), that is unable to activate NSF and promote SNARE complex disassembly, failed to reconstitute transferrin flux through the endocytic pathway (Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 3G and described in the text, with citation to Barnard et al., 1997.

claim: Reconstituting α-SNAP deficient cells with α-SNAP-L294A mutant fully restores SOCE.
source: Most importantly, reconstituting α-SNAP deficient cells with a previously reported mutant of α-SNAP, L294A (Barnard et al., 1997) (Figure 4A), that is unable to activate NSF and promote SNARE complex disassembly, failed to reconstitute transferrin flux through the endocytic pathway (Figure 3G) but fully restored SOCE (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3H and described in the text, with citation to Barnard et al., 1997.

claim: α-SNAP-L294A mutant co-immunoprecipitates Stim1.
source: Accordingly, like WT-α-SNAP, the L294A mutant co-immunoprecipitates Stim1 (Figure 3I) as well as Orai1 (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3I and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP-L294A mutant co-immunoprecipitates Orai1.
source: Accordingly, like WT-α-SNAP, the L294A mutant co-immunoprecipitates Stim1 (Figure 3I) as well as Orai1 (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3J and described in the text.

claim: The function of α-SNAP in SOCE is separate from its function in membrane trafficking.
source: This clearly separates the function of α-SNAP in SOCE from its function in membrane trafficking demonstrating that α-SNAP regulates SOCE by a novel mechanism that is independent of its role in bridging NSF to SNARE complexes and more sensitive to its depletion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that L294A mutant restores SOCE but not transferrin flux.

claim: α-SNAP regulates SOCE by a novel mechanism that is independent of its role in bridging NSF to SNARE complexes.
source: This clearly separates the function of α-SNAP in SOCE from its function in membrane trafficking demonstrating that α-SNAP regulates SOCE by a novel mechanism that is independent of its role in bridging NSF to SNARE complexes and more sensitive to its depletion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: Upon store-depletion, α-SNAP-NT but not α-SNAP-CT co-localizes with Stim1 clusters in CFP-Stim1 expressing cells.
source: In contrast, upon store-depletion, α-SNAP-NT but not α-SNAP-CT co-localized with Stim1 clusters in CFP-Stim1 expressing cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4B and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP-NT is able to partially restore SOCE in α-SNAP depleted cells.
source: Accordingly, α-SNAP-NT was able to partially restore SOCE in α-SNAP depleted cells (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C and described in the text.

claim: A specific domain within the N-terminal half (1–160 aa) of α-SNAP is crucial for binding to Stim1 and recruitment to the CRAC channel cluster.
source: Accordingly, α-SNAP-NT was able to partially restore SOCE in α-SNAP depleted cells (Figure 4C) suggesting that a specific domain within the N-terminal half (1–160 aa) of α-SNAP is crucial for binding to Stim1 and recruitment to the CRAC channel cluster.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that α-SNAP-NT co-localizes with Stim1 and partially restores SOCE.

claim: Reconstitution of α-SNAP deficient cells with α-SNAP-LOOP mutant is able to restore transferrin uptake and recycling.
source: Remarkably, reconstitution of α-SNAP deficient cells with this α-SNAP hydrophobic loop mutant (α-SNAP-LOOP) was able to restore transferrin uptake and recycling (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by transferrin uptake assay data shown in Figure 4D and described in the text.

claim: Reconstitution of α-SNAP deficient cells with α-SNAP-LOOP mutant fails to rescue SOCE.
source: Remarkably, reconstitution of α-SNAP deficient cells with this α-SNAP hydrophobic loop mutant (α-SNAP-LOOP) was able to restore transferrin uptake and recycling (Figure 4D) but failed to rescue SOCE (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP-LOOP shows significantly reduced binding to Stim1.
source: Accordingly, α-SNAP-LOOP showed significantly reduced binding to Stim1 (Figure 4F) and Orai1 (Figure 4G)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP-LOOP shows significantly reduced binding to Orai1.
source: Accordingly, α-SNAP-LOOP showed significantly reduced binding to Stim1 (Figure 4F) and Orai1 (Figure 4G)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP-LOOP fails to co-localize with Stim1 clusters in store-depleted HEK 293 cells stably expressing CFP-Stim1.
source: Accordingly, α-SNAP-LOOP showed significantly reduced binding to Stim1 (Figure 4F) and Orai1 (Figure 4G) and failed to co-localize with Stim1 clusters in store-depleted HEK 293 cells stably expressing CFP-Stim1 (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4H and described in the text.

claim: The domains of α-SNAP required for SOCE are different from those essential for NSF activation and SNARE complex disassembly.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that the domains of α-SNAP required for SOCE are different from those essential for NSF activation and SNARE complex disassembly, conclusively demonstrating a distinct role for α-SNAP in SOCE.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of α-SNAP mutants on SOCE and transferrin recycling.

claim: α-SNAP shows strong binding to the CAD domain of Stim1.
source: α-SNAP showed strong binding to the CAD domain of Stim1 and faint binding to the CAD plus CC1 domain (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5A and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP shows faint binding to the CAD plus CC1 domain of Stim1.
source: α-SNAP showed strong binding to the CAD domain of Stim1 and faint binding to the CAD plus CC1 domain (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5A and described in the text.

claim: Purified α-SNAP predominantly binds to the C-terminal tail of Orai1.
source: To identify the domains of Orai1 that bind α-SNAP, we tagged the cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails of Orai1 with GST, expressed them in E. coli and found that purified α-SNAP predominantly binds to the C-terminal tail of Orai1 (Orai1-CT) although faint binding to the N-terminal tail of Orai1 (Orai1-NT) was also detected (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5B and described in the text.

claim: Faint binding of purified α-SNAP to the N-terminal tail of Orai1 was detected.
source: To identify the domains of Orai1 that bind α-SNAP, we tagged the cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails of Orai1 with GST, expressed them in E. coli and found that purified α-SNAP predominantly binds to the C-terminal tail of Orai1 (Orai1-CT) although faint binding to the N-terminal tail of Orai1 (Orai1-NT) was also detected (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5B and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion causes significant inhibition of SOCE in cells co-expressing full length Stim1 and Orai1.
source: As expected, α-SNAP depletion caused significant inhibition of SOCE in cells co-expressing full length Stim1 and Orai1 (Figure 5C and 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and 5D and described in the text.

claim: SOCE in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1 is resistant to α-SNAP depletion.
source: However, SOCE in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1, although overall smaller, was resistant to α-SNAP depletion (Figure 5E and 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E and 5F and described in the text.

claim: Basal calcium levels in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1 are higher compared to WT HEK 293 cells.
source: Similarly, basal calcium levels in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1, although higher compared to WT HEK 293 cells, were unaffected by α-SNAP depletion (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium measurement data shown in Figure 5G and described in the text.

claim: Basal calcium levels in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1 are unaffected by α-SNAP depletion.
source: Similarly, basal calcium levels in cells co-expressing the cytosolic CAD fragment of Stim1 along with Orai1, although higher compared to WT HEK 293 cells, were unaffected by α-SNAP depletion (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium measurement data shown in Figure 5G and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP directly binds specific domains within Stim1 and Orai1 to enable a molecular step that precedes CAD mediated activation of SOCE in cells expressing full length Stim1.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that α-SNAP directly binds specific domains within Stim1 and Orai1 to enable a molecular step that precedes CAD mediated activation of SOCE in cells expressing full length Stim1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that CAD-mediated SOCE is resistant to α-SNAP depletion.

claim: The ability of Stim1 to oligomerize and translocate to the junctional ER upon store-depletion appears normal in α-SNAP deficient cells.
source: While the ability of Stim1 to oligomerize and translocate to the junctional ER upon store-depletion appeared normal in α-SNAP deficient cells, the size of Stim1-Orai1 clusters appeared larger (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: The size of Stim1-Orai1 clusters appears larger in α-SNAP deficient cells.
source: While the ability of Stim1 to oligomerize and translocate to the junctional ER upon store-depletion appeared normal in α-SNAP deficient cells, the size of Stim1-Orai1 clusters appeared larger (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion increases the overall size of CRAC channel clusters.
source: We adopted a localized thresholding method to detect Stim1-Orai1 cluster boundaries (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), used it to quantify the size and intensity of individual Stim1–Orai1 clusters, and found that α-SNAP depletion increased the overall size of CRAC channel clusters (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6B and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP depletion does not affect the density of Stim1 in junctional clusters.
source: We did not find an appreciable difference in the average intensity of CFP-Stim1 estimated from Stim1–Orai1 clusters in control or α-SNAP depleted, HEK 293 cells stably expressing CFP-Stim1 and Orai1-YFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). These data suggest that α-SNAP depletion does not affect the density of Stim1 in junctional clusters.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a significant increase in the average Orai1-YFP intensity in α-SNAP depleted clusters.
source: Surprisingly, we found a significant increase in the average Orai1-YFP intensity in α-SNAP depleted clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and described in the text.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all CRAC channel clusters in α-SNAP depleted cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found a significant increase in the average Orai1-YFP intensity in α-SNAP depleted clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), resulting in a significant decrease in the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all CRAC channel clusters (Figure 6C) as well as in the majority of individual clusters (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6C and described in the text.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) in the majority of individual clusters in α-SNAP depleted cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found a significant increase in the average Orai1-YFP intensity in α-SNAP depleted clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), resulting in a significant decrease in the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all CRAC channel clusters (Figure 6C) as well as in the majority of individual clusters (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6D and described in the text.

claim: α-SNAP regulates an active molecular rearrangement within CRAC channel clusters that is necessary for obtaining optimal Stim1/Orai1 ratios required for the physiological activation of SOCE through CRAC channels.
source: These changes and their inhibitory effect on SOCE (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) suggest that α-SNAP regulates an active molecular rearrangement within CRAC channel clusters that is necessary for obtaining optimal Stim1/Orai1 ratios required for the physiological activation of SOCE through CRAC channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing changes in Stim1/Orai1 ratios and their correlation with SOCE.

claim: The amplitude of calcium selective CRAC currents correlates well with the ratio of Stim1 to Orai1 or CAD to Orai1 within CRAC channel complex.
source: Indeed, two independent recent studies that experimentally manipulated Stim1:Orai1 ratios in junctional clusters showed that the amplitude of calcium selective CRAC currents correlates well with the ratio of Stim1 to Orai1 or CAD to Orai1 within CRAC channel complex (Mcnally et al., 2012; Hoover and Lewis, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two independent studies (Mcnally et al., 2012; Hoover and Lewis, 2011).

claim: Over-expression of α-SNAP enhances SOCE beyond what is typically seen in cells stably co-expressing Stim1 and Orai1.
source: Remarkably, over-expression of α-SNAP enhanced SOCE beyond what is typically seen in cells stably co-expressing Stim1 and Orai1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and described in the text.

claim: Over-expression of α-SNAP significantly enhances the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all junctional clusters.
source: Concomitant with an increase in SOCE, over-expression of α-SNAP significantly enhanced the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all junctional clusters (Figure 6E) as well as majority of individual clusters (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6E and described in the text.

claim: Over-expression of α-SNAP significantly enhances the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) in the majority of individual clusters.
source: Concomitant with an increase in SOCE, over-expression of α-SNAP significantly enhanced the ratio of CFP (Stim1) to YFP (Orai1) across all junctional clusters (Figure 6E) as well as majority of individual clusters (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 6F and described in the text.

claim: Over-expression of α-SNAP does not affect total surface Orai1 levels in resting or store-depleted cells.
source: Notably, over-expression of α-SNAP did not affect total surface Orai1 levels in resting or store-depleted cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 5) or average CFP-Stim1 intensity per cell (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by BTX binding assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and described in the text.

claim: Over-expression of α-SNAP does not affect average CFP-Stim1 intensity per cell.
source: Notably, over-expression of α-SNAP did not affect total surface Orai1 levels in resting or store-depleted cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 5) or average CFP-Stim1 intensity per cell (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: α-SNAP directly binds Stim1 and Orai1 and co-localizes with CRAC channel clusters in the junctional ER.
source: In summary we have shown that α-SNAP directly binds Stim1 and Orai1 and co-localizes with CRAC channel clusters in the junctional ER.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within CRAC channel clusters, α-SNAP enables a crucial and previously unknown molecular re-arrangement that results in optimal Stim1:Orai1 ratios necessary for the physiological activation of SOCE.
source: Within CRAC channel clusters, α-SNAP enables a crucial and previously unknown molecular re-arrangement that results in optimal Stim1:Orai1 ratios necessary for the physiological activation of SOCE (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data and inference presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulation of SOCE by α-SNAP is completely independent of its well-known role in NSF mediated SNARE complex disassembly.
source: Regulation of SOCE by α-SNAP is completely independent of its well-known role in NSF mediated SNARE complex disassembly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that NSF inhibition does not affect SOCE and that α-SNAP mutants unable to activate NSF can still restore SOCE.

claim: Stim1–Orai1 clustering at ER–PM junctions is insufficient to fully activate SOCE unless followed by a α-SNAP dependent active molecular re-arrangement within CRAC channel clusters.
source: We demonstrate that Stim1–Orai1 clustering at ER–PM junctions is insufficient to fully activate SOCE unless followed by a α-SNAP dependent active molecular re-arrangement within CRAC channel clusters.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Stim1-Orai1 clustering occurs in α-SNAP depleted cells but SOCE is inhibited.

claim: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) by calcium release activated calcium (CRAC) channels constitutes a primary route of calcium entry in most cells.
